questions.q: Make it negative: « Je vais quelque part ce week-end. »
choices: Je ne vais pas quelque part ce week-end.
Je ne vais nulle part ce week-end.
Je vais nulle part ce week-end.
Je ne vais rien ce week-end.
questions.why: Each positive has its own negative partner: quelqu'un → personne, quelque chose → rien, quelque part → nulle part. The partner replaces pas, it does not join it.

questions.q: Make it negative: « Quelque chose a changé. » → ___ n'a changé.
questions.why: Rien and personne can be the subject, and then they come first. The ne stays where it always is, in front of the verb, with nothing behind it.

questions.q: Which sentence means « It's nothing serious » ?
choices: Ce n'est pas rien de grave.
questions.why: An adjective hung on rien, quelque chose, quelqu'un or personne is joined by de. English joins them with nothing at all, which is why the de goes missing.
The linking de elides before a vowel, exactly as elsewhere: quelqu'un d'important, personne d'autre, rien d'utile.

questions.q: Put « belle » in the form this sentence needs: « Elle a dit quelque chose de ___ . »
questions.why: After that de the adjective is always bare masculine singular, whatever it describes. Quelqu'un de gentil is said of a woman too; only quelques-unes, a real plural, forces agreement.
The head of tout le monde is monde, a singular noun, so the verb is singular however plural the meaning feels. Chacun behaves the same way: chacun fait ce qu'il veut.
As a subject, personne takes the front slot and the ne still leans on the verb. Nothing follows it, because personne is itself the second half of the negation.

questions.q: Complete: « Prends ___ . » (Take any one of them; the noun has already been said.)
questions.why: Quel is a determiner and needs its noun beside it; lequel is the pronoun that stands in for a noun already mentioned. Same division as the plain quel / lequel pair.
Here the noun heure is present, so quel is used and agrees with it: feminine singular. With a plural noun it would be n'importe quels jours.

questions.q: A French friend says « Il dit n'importe quoi. » What does he mean?
choices: He'll say whatever you ask him to
questions.why: N'importe has a neutral reading (prends n'importe lequel, any of them will do) and a dismissive one. With dire, raconter or faire it is almost always the dismissive one: c'est n'importe quoi.

questions.q: Which sentence means « Each one has their own book » ?
questions.why: Chaque is a determiner and cannot stand without its noun; chacun is the pronoun that replaces it. Both are singular, and chaque has no plural at all.

questions.q: Complete: « Je n'ai lu ___ de ces pages. » (not one of them)
questions.why: Rien is a pronoun that replaces a whole thing; aucun points back at a noun and agrees with it. Pages is feminine, so aucune. Je n'ai rien lu would say nothing about which pages.

questions.q: Build the sentence: There's nobody else here.
questions.why: Autre is an adjective, so it needs the linking de, elided before its vowel. The ne of il n'y a is what makes personne negative rather than a noun.

questions.q: Type what you hear, in correct written French.
questions.why: Two negative words, one ne: the subject personne takes the front, rien is a light word so it lands before the participle. Compare je n'ai vu personne, where the heavy word follows it.

questions.q: Say the everyday way of dismissing something as nonsense.
questions.why: This is the phrase you will hear daily, about a film, an argument or a decision. Its neutral twin, n'importe quoi meaning anything at all, is the same words with a different job.

questions.q: Explain how an adjective attaches to quelque chose, rien, quelqu'un and personne. Give the rule, its two mistakes, and one example each.
a: The adjective is joined by de (d' before a vowel) and stays masculine singular: quelque chose de beau, rien de grave, quelqu'un d'intéressant, personne d'autre. Mistake one is dropping the de (quelque chose beau); mistake two is making the adjective agree (quelqu'un d'intelligente). An infinitive takes à instead: quelque chose à manger, rien à faire.
questions.why: The de is invisible in English, so it disappears; the agreement is so drilled elsewhere that it leaks in here. Knowing both failure modes is what stops them.
